name: Sayre's Law
statement: In any dispute, the intensity of feeling is inversely proportional to the value of the issues at stake.
meaning: The smaller and less consequential the matter, the more ferociously people tend to fight over it. Its famous corollary: that is why academic politics are so bitter, because the stakes are so low.
mechanism: Low-stakes issues lack any objective way to settle them, so argument runs unchecked. With little material on the line, the dispute becomes a proxy for status, competence, and being right rather than about the object itself. And everyone feels qualified to weigh in on something small and simple (where a large, complex matter intimidates people into deference), so the trivial issue draws the most voices and the most heat.

examples.text: A department spends far longer disputing a course title or a seminar-room assignment than approving a large budget. The low-stakes items invite everyone's opinion and quietly become contests over standing.

The overlap with Parkinson's law of triviality: a committee waves through a costly, complex contract in minutes but argues at length over a trivial, easily-pictured item everyone feels entitled to judge.
Disputes over fence heights, lawn ornaments, or newsletter fonts routinely escalate to intense personal conflict despite almost no practical consequence: Sayre's law in the wild.

variants.name: The narcissism of small differences
variants.text: Freud's related observation (1930): communities with adjoining, minimally-different identities are especially prone to feuding (small differences, not large ones, breed the fiercest antagonism).

variants.name: A tangle of claimants
variants.text: The quip has been attributed to Henry Kissinger, Woodrow Wilson, Laurence Peter and others as well as Sayre: a small dispute over a small saying that rather proves its own point.

whyItMatters: It is a diagnostic for group dysfunction: when a meeting overheats, the temperature is often a sign the issue is trivial, not vital. Naming the pattern lets a chair protect real decisions from being crowded out by the ones everybody has an opinion on.

working.lead: Read heat as a signal of low stakes
working.text: when a discussion turns unexpectedly bitter, ask whether the ferocity is tracking importance — often it is tracking the opposite.
put a clock on cheap, easily-understood items so they cannot expand to consume the meeting; reserve real time for the decisions that matter.
much low-stakes heat is a proxy contest over standing; naming that, gently, can defuse it faster than arguing the object.

limits: It is a humorous aphorism, not a measured finding ('inversely proportional' is rhetorical, not quantified) and it plainly fails as a universal law, since high-stakes disputes (wars, existential business fights) are also intensely emotional. Its attribution is genuinely disputed and poorly documented. It captures a recognisable pattern in low-stakes group conflict; it is not a rule you could plot on a graph.
misreadings: It does not claim that people never care about big things, only that trivial disputes attract a disproportionate ferocity. Read as a strict inverse law it is false; read as a caution about where committee energy really goes, it is sharp.
origin: Named for Wallace Stanley Sayre (1905–1972), a political scientist at Columbia University, who is said to have used the quip from around the 1950s. The best-known corollary (that academic politics are so vicious 'because the stakes are so low') was recorded in the Wall Street Journal in 1973, and the economist Charles Philip Issawi published the maxim as 'Sayre's Law' the same year. Its attribution is famously tangled, with versions credited to Kissinger, Woodrow Wilson, and others.

sources.text: Sayre's law, Wikipedia. — the wording, Sayre's biography, the 1973 attribution, and the rival claimants.
"Academic Politics Are So Vicious Because the Stakes Are So Small." Quote Investigator (2013). — the dated attribution history from Samuel Johnson (1765) to Issawi (1973).
